paras: The lynching of John Henderson took place in the early hours of August 21, 1890, when masked men took Henderson, a Black prisoner, from the Woodford County jail at Versailles, Kentucky, and hanged him from a tree. He had been accused of killing Gilbert Satterwhite, a white farmer, near Midway three days earlier. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of persons unknown, and a Kentucky paper condemned the lynching and the jailer who allowed it.

Satterwhite had hired Henderson's wife to keep house while his own family was away, and on the night of Monday, August 18, he set out for Midway with her in his buggy. He was later found dead in the road, shot through the head and slashed with a razor, and Henderson, a former hand he had discharged, was arrested. According to a Lexington dispatch, Henderson told a Midway doctor, who treated a bullet wound in his shoulder, that he had found Satterwhite with his wife, had been shot when he grappled with him, and had then attacked him. Neighbors rejected the story as cover for revenge over his dismissal, and there was "strong talk of lynching him."

During a rainstorm early on Thursday, August 21, callers woke the jailer, R. W. Shipp, claiming to bring a prisoner from Frankfort. When the deputy, Ed Yogel, opened the door, a man held a pistol on him and took the keys, and about fifteen masked men entered; the Evening World's correspondent wrote that Henderson stepped out and declared he had killed Satterwhite. Joined outside by ten or fifteen more, the men took him about a mile out the Frankfort pike and, after letting him pray, hanged him from a locust tree in front of G. M. Fishback's house.

Fishback found the body at 5 a.m. and notified the sheriff, and the coroner's jury returned a verdict of death "at the hands of persons unknown"; Henderson was buried at county expense. No report of an arrest of any member of the mob was found. Henderson's wife was held as an accessory, and the wire said another Black man had been arrested as an accessory and would probably be hanged; the coverage does not show what became of either. White papers reported Black residents of Versailles and Midway "very much excited" and, according to the wire, threatening to avenge the hanging on whites.

The story reached readers mainly through a Midway wire dated August 21, printed on August 22 in New York, St. Paul, Fort Worth, Wheeling and Savannah and later in weekly digests in Kansas, Delaware and North Carolina. The wire treated Henderson's guilt as proven, calling him "the miserable wretch" and saying he "confessed the killing"; headlines ran from "Murderer Henderson Lynched by Indignant Kentuckians" to "Judge Lynch Hustles a Negro Off Kentucky Soil."

The New York Evening World ran the fullest account, a Lexington special headlined "A Brutal Negro Hanged by a Mob in Kentucky" that narrated the hanging as a scene of prayer and lightning. Its subhead read "Fears That the Blacks Will Retaliate Upon the Lynchers," and the story closed on that fear rather than on the mob. As late as August 27 a Michigan weekly was printing Henderson's self-defense story under "Cut Off His Enemy's Head."

The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford, Kentucky, took a different line, calling the lynching "not only an unnecessary but a very reprehensible act," noting that the prisoner was in custody and certain of execution, and charging that the Woodford jailer "admitted the mob with not even a feigned obstruction." The Washington National Tribune, by contrast, used the case for a joke about Kentucky's murder rate. No Black-press account of the lynching was found.

Early dispatches and the Evening World date the killing to Monday night, the wire and the Interior Journal to Tuesday; the Weekly Courier-Journal alone dated the lynching to "Tuesday night." The wire placed the hanging "in the edge of town," while the Lexington special put it a mile from the Versailles jail, and two Kansas digests misprinted the town as "Midland." Reports of a confession come from accounts of the mob's actions and conflict with one another.

reader.title: Lynching of John Henderson
bases: Masked men took John Henderson, a Black prisoner accused of murder, from the Woodford County jail and hanged him from a tree (A4, A5, A14).

Henderson was hanged by some twenty-five or more masked men who took him from jail without any legal authority (A4, A14); they acted on the accusation that he had murdered a white farmer, and a Kentucky editor noted he 'was in custody and as sure of judicial execution as anything could be' (A16).
A Lexington special (A4), the Midway wire (A5), a Versailles dispatch (A14) and the Louisville Courier-Journal (A15) independently report that a mob took Henderson from jail and hanged him.

accounts.label: Henderson's account (to the doctor)
accounts.gist: He said he found Satterwhite with his wife by the roadside, was shot in the shoulder when he grappled with him, then cut him with a razor and shot him with his own pistol.

accounts.label: Neighbors' version
accounts.gist: Satterwhite's neighbors disbelieved Henderson, saying he took revenge for being discharged and shot himself to support his story.

accounts.label: Midway wire
accounts.gist: Henderson 'confessed the killing' but did not know why; he and another Black man killed Satterwhite for discharging them from a threshing gang; a mob took him from jail about 2 a.m. and hanged him at the edge of town.

accounts.label: Lexington special to the Evening World
accounts.gist: About fifteen masked men tricked and disarmed the deputy jailer, took Henderson, who admitted the killing in the jail, and hanged him a mile out the Frankfort pike after letting him pray; at the tree he made no confession.

accounts.label: Kentucky editorial
accounts.gist: The Stanford Interior Journal called the lynching unnecessary and reprehensible and said the jailer admitted the mob without resistance.

framing.detail: The Midway wire, run with headlines such as 'Strung Up to a Tree' and 'Judge Lynch Hustles a Negro Off Kentucky Soil,' treated Henderson's guilt as settled and called him 'the miserable wretch.'
The Evening World headlined 'A Brutal Negro Hanged by a Mob' and 'Fears That the Blacks Will Retaliate,' narrating the hanging in detail without comment on the mob.
The Stanford Interior Journal called the lynching 'unnecessary' and 'very reprehensible' and blamed the Woodford jailer.
The National Tribune folded the lynching into a jibe at Kentucky's murder rate.

record_check.dossier: The alleged murder was near Midway; Henderson was held in the Woodford County jail at Versailles and hanged about a mile out the Frankfort pike from there. The Midway wire's 'edge of town' is less specific.
The lynching killed one person (Henderson). Satterwhite's death was the alleged crime; if counted, white_killed should be 1 rather than null.

record_check.record: about twenty-five masked men ... hanged him from a locust tree near Versailles
record_check.dossier: About fifteen men entered the jail and ten or fifteen more joined outside (25-30 in all); the deputy was held at pistol point.
Correct for deaths. Henderson's wife was jailed as an accessory, and the wire reported another Black man arrested and threatened with lynching; no report of what happened to either was found.
At least 20 white papers carried it from August 20 to September 17, including Kentucky papers; no Black-press account was found.

info: Henderson was taken from jail and hanged in the early morning of Thursday, August 21, 1890, between about 2 and 3 a.m.

Taken from the Woodford County jail at Versailles and hanged from a locust tree in front of G. M. Fishback's residence, about a mile out the Frankfort pike; the Midway wire says 'in the edge of town.'
John Henderson, described as a 'negro' and 'colored'; formerly employed by Satterwhite.
Accused of killing Gilbert H. Satterwhite, a white farmer, on the road near Midway, by shooting him and cutting him with a razor, on Monday night, August 18 (Tuesday in two reports).
Masked men, unidentified; they arrived and left on horseback.
